name: Many Perfect Squares
description: You are given a set $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ of distinct positive integers. We define the squareness of an integer $$$x$$$ as the number of perfect squares among the numbers $$$a_1 + x, a_2 + x, \ldots, a_n + x$$$. Find the maximum squareness among all integers $$$x$$$ between $$$0$$$ and $$$10^{18}$$$, inclusive. Perfect squares are integers of the form $$$t^2$$$, where $$$t$$$ is a non-negative integer. The smallest perfect squares are $$$0, 1, 4, 9, 16, \ldots$$$.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 50$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 50$$$) — the size of the set. The second line contains $$$n$$$ distinct integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ in increasing order ($$$1 \le a_1 \lt a_2 \lt \ldots \lt a_n \le 10^9$$$) — the set itself. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$50$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print a single integer — the largest possible number of perfect squares among $$$a_1 + x, a_2 + x, \ldots, a_n + x$$$, for some $$$0 \le x \le 10^{18}$$$.
approach_summary: Precompute linear sieve to store minimum prime factor (spf[x]) up to N in O(N). Factorize any number x ≤ N in O(log x) steps.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1781D — Many Perfect Squares [242. Sieve, Prime Factorization and Divisors]
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Every composite integer $X$ has at least one prime factor $\le \sqrt{X}$. Precomputing the Smallest Prime Factor (SPF) for all numbers up to $M$ via a linear sieve allows any $X \le M$ to be completely prime-factorized in $O(\log X)$ steps.
